entities.summary:
The Forbidden City, constructed between 1406 and 1420, served as the imperial palace for the Ming and Qing dynasties in Beijing, China. Spanning approximately 180 acres, it is a masterpiece of traditional Chinese palatial architecture, symbolizing the zenith of imperial power and cultural sophistication. As a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it stands as a testament to China's historical and cultural heritage, influencing architecture, governance, and art across East Asia and beyond.

The construction of the Forbidden City was ordered by the Yongle Emperor, the third emperor of the Ming dynasty, who sought to establish a centralized imperial authority. The complex consists of around 980 buildings, characterized by their grand scale, intricate designs, and harmonious layout. It served as the political and ritual center of Chinese government for nearly 500 years, hosting significant events such as imperial ceremonies, state banquets, and diplomatic meetings, effectively shaping the governance of one of history's longest-lasting empires.

The legacy of the Forbidden City extends far beyond its architectural significance; it has become a symbol of Chinese identity and cultural pride. Following the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, the palace complex transitioned into a museum, opening its doors to the public in 1925. Its influence can be seen in various aspects of Chinese culture, from literature and art to modern architecture, and it continues to attract millions of visitors each year, serving as a vital link to understanding China's imperial past.

As a striking reminder of its historical importance, it is estimated that over 19 million people visit the Forbidden City annually, reflecting its status as one of the most visited cultural sites in the world, encapsulating the enduring allure of China's imperial history.
